sentences.text: Nél was eleven and had recently become the sort of person who wanted the rule stated properly.
She got a lot of different answers.
The clearest came from Dona Lurdes at the café, who had been in that harbour since 1961 and who set it out for her over a cup of milky coffee that Nél had not asked for and drank anyway.
The rule, said Dona Lurdes, was this.
The gull does not bring you things.
The gull brings back things.
There is an enormous difference and half the town gets it wrong.
Everything on that bollard, ever, has been something the sea took off somebody.
Not something lost inland and washed down the river.
Not something dropped on the beach.
Something the water took: off a boat, off the wall, out of a pocket in a swell.
"And she brings it back?" "She puts it where a person can find it.
That's all I'll say she does.
What you make of that is your affair." Nél asked how long the gull had been doing it, expecting an answer in years.
Dona Lurdes said that was the wrong question and that Nél was clever enough to work out why, which took Nél about four seconds and then made her sit back in her chair.
Gulls live for twenty or thirty years.
Some go longer.
Not seventy.
"So it's not the same gull." "No." "Then who taught it?" Dona Lurdes drank her coffee.
"That," she said, "is the question I have been not answering for sixty years, and I am not going to spoil my record for you."
